Where it began

Rod Marsh was born in Armadale, a suburb of Perth, on 4 November 1947. His first opponent was his older brother Graham, in the backyard; Graham went on to a fine career as a professional golfer, with eleven wins on the European Tour. Both boys played schoolboy cricket for Western Australia.

Rod was keeping wicket at eight and captaining the state schoolboys at thirteen. He came into the Western Australia side as a batsman, and on his debut against the West Indies in 1968–69 he hit 104 off an attack that included Garfield Sobers and Wes Hall.

The player

He was picked for Australia in the 1970–71 Ashes, partly for his batting, and his keeping took a while to win the critics round. It got there in the end. He played 96 Tests from 1970 to 1984, taking 343 catches and 12 stumpings, and his 355 dismissals were a world record when he retired. He was the first keeper to reach 350.

He could bat, too. In 1972–73 he became the first Australian keeper to make a Test hundred, and at the Centenary Test in 1977 he made an unbeaten 110 against England. In all he scored 3,633 Test runs, with three hundreds and 16 fifties.

What made him special

Powerfully built but quick on his feet, he made keeping a spectacle: diving catches, loud appeals and the ball tossed high into the air after a dismissal. His understanding with Dennis Lillee, his friend from club cricket in Perth, was close to telepathic, and Lillee's bowling and Marsh's gloves combined for 95 Test wickets. The two arrived in the same series and left in the same match.

He also put the team first. In 1970–71 his captain declared with Marsh on 92, eight short of a hundred; Marsh said he had gained forty runs rather than lost eight.

Away from the middle

After playing he commentated for Channel Nine and then ran the Australian Cricket Academy, where his pupils included Adam Gilchrist, Jason Gillespie and Brett Lee. He went on to lead the England and Wales national academy from 2001 to 2005 and later chaired Australia's selectors.

He was made an MBE in 1982, named a Wisden Cricketer of the Year the same year and entered the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame in 2009. He died in 2022, aged 74.

And finally

He was the man who led Australia's dressing room in its team song, Under the Southern Cross I Stand, and when he retired he handed the job to Allan Border. A keeper who missed little, and who made sure the winning team was always heard.
